content:
Whitney kept her own three opening lines and the "hard truth" framing, and the approved version says couples are searching and finding competitors first, even less qualified ones. It is blunt and competitive.

Candidate A changes line three, drops "if ideal couples can't find you on Google" and the hard-truth line, and softens the message. It says competitors aren't better, which partly echoes "less qualified," but the tone is gentle and reflective. It never mentions Google Ads or WIA. It does include the "missing from Google searches" idea, and its ending, "may not require getting better," is a decent angle but diverges from the punchy approach.

Candidate B also changes line three and drops the hard truth. It keeps "if ideal couples can't find you on Google," which Whitney had in her draft. It adds a WIA pitch about Google Ads, which was not requested for this piece and may be premature. It lacks the competitor-winning urgency and the "high-intent leads" idea, though "actively searching" is close.

Both miss the hard truth. A is longer and more philosophical, with no sense of competitors winning. B is shorter and keeps more of her structure, but its Google Ads pitch is an unrequested addition. A's "That doesn't mean your competitors are better" gets closer to the reference's point that less qualified competitors win simply because they're easier to find. Still, A reads as more rewritten. B would need cutting the pitch paragraph and adding the competitor line, but its first sentence after the opener is closer to her wording.

Neither is great. B keeps more of her wording and has the "actively searching" idea, so I lean B, though A's competitor point is closer in substance.

request.system:
You compare two draft pieces of marketing copy for Wedding Industry Ads (WIA), a wedding-industry advertising agency. You are given the request, the version WIA's co-founder Whitney actually approved or wrote (the reference), and two candidate drafts. Decide which candidate would need fewer and smaller edits to become something Whitney would approve. Judge substance first (what is claimed, for whom, how WIA is positioned, accuracy, whether her own wording was kept where she supplied it), then voice. Do not reward length, and do not require the candidate to copy the reference wording.

Return only JSON: {"winner": "A" or "B" or "tie", "edits_needed_A": "few", "edits_needed_B": "many", "reason": "one or two sentences"} where edits_needed values are none, few, some or many.
request.user:
Request:
Thoughts on the following? And don't just inflate my ego. You need to help me reach my ultimate potential

You’re the venue couples dream about.
You’re the planner who overdelivers.
You’re the creative who makes wedding day magic.

But if ideal couples can't find you on Google, you're falling short of your true potential.

Here’s the hard truth you may not want to hear:

Your strongest competitors are booking couples who would have been perfect for you because the clients found them on Google first.

Reference (what Whitney approved):
You’re the venue couples dream about.
You’re the planner who overdelivers.
You’re the creative who makes wedding day magic.

But if ideal couples can’t find you on Google, you’re missing out on ready-to-book, high-intent leads.

Here’s the hard truth you may not want to hear:
Couples are searching. And they’re finding your competitors first.
Even the less qualified ones are winning bookings...simply because they’re easier to find.

Candidate A:
You’re the venue couples dream about.
You’re the planner who overdelivers.
You’re the creative who brings their vision to life.

But couples can’t choose a business they never discover.

You can have an exceptional reputation, a beautiful website, and a client experience people rave about—and still be missing from the Google searches that put other businesses on a couple’s shortlist.

That doesn’t mean your competitors are better at what they do.

It means they have an opportunity to earn trust before you’re even part of the conversation.

Your next stage of growth may not require getting better at serving your couples.

It may require being more intentional about how the right couples find you.

Candidate B:
You’re the venue couples dream about.
You’re the planner who overdelivers.
You’re the creative whose work gets remembered long after the wedding.

But if ideal couples can’t find you on Google, they may never know you’re an option.

When a couple searches for a venue or wedding pro, the businesses they find have an opportunity to earn their inquiry. Yours deserves to be part of that decision.

That’s where we focus with Google Ads: building on your existing marketing to put your business in front of couples actively searching for what you offer, with a clear reason to inquire.
